canonical.title: Pure React 19 SPA or a .NET 10 BFF? A decision framework for an internal admin console

children.title: In-memory tokens vs cookie-backed BFF sessions under XSS: what each architecture actually buys you
children.summary: httpOnly cookies do not stop XSS — they convert silent token exfiltration into loud, tab-bound session riding. That's a real but bounded win; CSP + Trusted Types is the actual mitigation.

children.title: Does the IETF browser-based-apps BCP apply to an internal admin console?
children.summary: The BCP names "business applications" in its strongest recommendation, so an internal console is in scope — but the ranking is a security/simplicity trade-off, not a normative MUST.

children.title: Refresh tokens and silent renew in a browser SPA (2026)
children.summary: Iframe silent renew is dead cross-site but alive same-site; refresh-token rotation works on both stacks, DPoP only really works on Keycloak, and TanStack Query needs a single-flight mutex either way.

children.title: Greenfield BFF vs retrofitting later: where the asymmetry actually is
children.summary: Adding a BFF later is a two-way door — if you build the SPA with one auth module, one fetch wrapper, relative paths and no client-side JWT parsing. The one-way door is the API, not the frontend.

children.title: What a BFF costs you every day: OpenAPI codegen and the local dev loop
children.summary: A path-preserving BFF leaves OpenAPI codegen essentially untouched — the real daily cost is one extra process, a Vite proxy config, and losing Swagger UI 'Try it out'.

children.title: BFF options in .NET 10: Duende.BFF, YARP, or hand-rolled
children.summary: If you build a BFF, the realistic .NET 10 choice is YARP + AddOpenIdConnect + the free Apache-2.0 Duende.AccessTokenManagement (~250 LOC you own), or Duende.BFF if you qualify for its free Community Edition; Duende.BFF's paid entry point is $5,750/yr.

sources.title: Duende BFF — Remote APIs
sources.claim: Duende BFF's remote-API forwarder uses YARP internally; the BFF authenticates the frontend with a cookie, obtains the access token and forwards it to the remote API — so the remote API keeps its bearer-token contract unchanged.

sources.title: Curity — Token Handler: the SPA's new BFF
sources.claim: The token handler / BFF pattern requires minimal changes to existing APIs because they keep receiving bearer tokens; the SPA's security code is simplified.

sources.title: IETF draft-ietf-oauth-browser-based-apps-27
sources.claim: The BCP's strongest recommendation names business applications explicitly: "strongly recommended for business applications, sensitive applications, and applications that handle personal data."

sources.title: IETF BCP (archive HTML) — architecture ranking
sources.claim: The BCP frames its architecture ranking as "a different trade-off between security and simplicity", in decreasing order of security, with no RFC 2119 keyword attached.

sources.title: FusionAuth — BFF security architecture
sources.claim: BFF's only remaining XSS vector is request proxying / session riding: the attacker can make requests while the browser is open, but cannot exfiltrate tokens for offline use. The Sept 2025 npm supply-chain compromise showed malicious JS can steal anything JS can read.

sources.title: Auth0 — what developers get wrong about BFF
sources.claim: "BFF shifts the security boundary. It doesn't eliminate it." Tokens in memory are as reachable as tokens in localStorage; the trade is XSS token theft for a more constrained CSRF surface.

sources.title: URIports — CSP and Trusted Types
sources.claim: Trusted Types enforces safe DOM manipulation at the sink level; Safari 26 (Sept 2025) and Firefox (Feb 2026) shipped it, at which point Trusted Types reached Baseline.

sources.title: Google / ACM CCS 2016 — CSP is Dead, Long Live CSP
sources.claim: Internet-scale study: 94.68% of policies that attempt to limit script execution are ineffective; allowlist-based CSP is largely bypassable.

sources.title: oidc-spa — third-party cookies and session restoration
sources.claim: Hosting app and IdP under the same registrable domain keeps the IdP first-party and lets iframe-based silent session restoration work; cross-site it does not, and the library falls back to a full-page redirect.

sources.title: web.dev — same-site vs same-origin
sources.claim: A 'site' is scheme + eTLD+1; different subdomains of the same registrable domain are same-site.

sources.title: Duende — managing OpenAPI specs with a BFF
sources.claim: A composing BFF requires transforming downstream OpenAPI specs: rewrite paths to the BFF prefix, rewrite servers to the BFF host, merge downstream docs, strip security schemes, add an X-CSRF interceptor.

sources.title: Duende BFF — server-side sessions
sources.claim: Server-side sessions keep the cookie small and constant and allow revocation on back-channel logout; they require a session store.

sources.title: Duende Support #972 — SignalR through the BFF
sources.claim: SignalR WebSocket and SSE transports fail through the Duende BFF forwarder because the WebSocket handshake cannot carry the required X-CSRF header; teams fall back to long-polling.

sources.title: Duende — pricing
sources.claim: Duende 2026 list prices: Lite $5,750/yr, Standard $12,500/yr, Advanced $24,900/yr. Free for development, testing and personal projects; only pay for production.

sources.title: Duende — Community Edition
sources.claim: Community Edition eligibility is revenue-based: <$1M USD projected annual gross revenue and <$3M USD capital. The gate is org revenue, not app audience.

sources.title: DuendeSoftware/foss
sources.claim: Duende.AccessTokenManagement and the other Duende FOSS libraries are Apache-2.0 licensed and free.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn — .NET 10 cookie auth 401/403 for API endpoints
sources.claim: Starting in .NET 10, unauthenticated requests to known API endpoints result in 401/403 rather than redirecting to a login URI.

sources.title: dotnet/aspnetcore #8175 — OAuth 2 refresh token support
sources.claim: Built-in OAuth 2 refresh-token support in ASP.NET Core is still an open issue (opened 2019), now milestoned .NET 11 Planning.

sources.title: dotnet/yarp
sources.claim: YARP is an MIT-licensed reverse-proxy toolkit from Microsoft, latest 2.3.0; its README does not cover authentication.

sources.title: Duende — licensing
sources.claim: Duende BFF requires a licence for production; trial mode limits to five sessions per host.

sources.title: Wrapt — standalone Duende BFF for any SPA
sources.claim: A standalone Duende BFF for a React SPA against Keycloak is ~50 lines of Program.cs; the dev setup runs two processes and proxies four routes.

sources.title: Microsoft .NET 10 BFF sample — CookieOidcRefresher.cs
sources.claim: Microsoft's CookieOidcRefresher is 102 lines of hand-written refresh logic with no locking/single-flight, and its header comment links to dotnet/aspnetcore#8175.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn — Data Protection key storage providers
sources.claim: Multi-instance cookie auth requires a shared Data Protection key ring (Redis, Azure Blob, Key Vault or SQL) so cookies encrypted by one instance can be read by another.

sources.title: thoughtbot — one-way vs two-way door decisions
sources.claim: One-way-door decisions are costly to reverse and warrant deliberation; two-way-door decisions should be made fast and iterated on.

sources.title: oidc-spa — the JWT of the access token
sources.claim: The access token is meant to be opaque to the client; decoding it in frontend code to read claims is discouraged.

sources.title: Vite — server options
sources.claim: Vite's dev server can proxy path prefixes such as /api and /bff to a backend, which is how a relative-path SPA runs against a BFF locally.

sources.title: Swagger — cookie authentication
sources.claim: Swagger UI cannot exercise cookie-authenticated endpoints via 'Try it out'.

sources.title: openapi-fetch — API
sources.claim: openapi-fetch's createClient accepts baseUrl plus any valid fetch option, so cookie auth under a BFF is a two-line change (baseUrl + credentials:'include').

sources.title: NSwag #5229 — WithCredentials not emitted
sources.claim: NSwag's WithCredentials = true does not emit credentials into the generated Fetch-template TypeScript client; use UseTransformOptionsMethod instead.

sources.title: Keycloak — DPoP support in 26.4
sources.claim: DPoP became an officially supported (no longer preview) Keycloak feature in 26.4, including binding refresh tokens for public clients.

sources.title: TanStack Query #6249 — concurrent 401s
sources.claim: Concurrent queries each hitting 401 fire duplicate refresh calls; the async-mutex / single-flight question in TanStack Query remains unanswered.

sources.title: RFC 9700 (BCP 240) — OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice
sources.claim: Refresh tokens issued to public clients must be sender-constrained or rotated, with reuse detection revoking the token family.

sources.title: Keycloak — JavaScript adapter
sources.claim: Keycloak documents that the Session Status iframe and silent check-sso are unsupported when third-party cookies are blocked.

sources.title: InfoQ — DPoP key storage, an unsolved problem
sources.claim: A non-extractable WebCrypto key still leaves a signing oracle reachable from XSS; Firefox cannot persist CryptoKey objects in IndexedDB.

sources.title: Pragmatic Web Security — localStorage is not the problem
sources.claim: Philippe De Ryck: avoiding localStorage is the wrong fix — XSS gives full control over application code, so in-memory / worker-hidden tokens are also reachable.

sources.title: OWASP — HTML5 Security Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Do not store session identifiers in local storage; a single XSS can steal everything in Web Storage.

sources.title: web.dev — strict CSP
sources.claim: Nonce/hash-based strict CSP with strict-dynamic blocks untrusted inline scripts, but does not stop injections into an already-nonced bundle.

sources.title: dotnet/aspnetcore #58016 — DPoP support
sources.claim: DPoP support in ASP.NET Core is still open and milestoned .NET 11 Planning; the only current options are Duende libraries or writing your own.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn — ASP.NET Core authentication
sources.claim: ASP.NET Core can register cookie and JWT bearer handlers side by side and require any one of multiple schemes, so one API can serve both browser and bearer clients.
